translations.text: The holy place of Saint Michael, on the mountain that is called Garganus, is known to many people.
The mountain stands on the borders of the land of Campania, by the Adriatic Sea, twelve miles' climb from a city called Siponto.
From that place the feast of this day was established throughout the faithful Church. A very wealthy man called Garganus lived there, and the mountain was named after what happened to him.
It happened, when the enormous multitude of his cattle was grazing on the mountain, that a certain proud bull went off alone and scorned the herd's drove.

So the lord Garganus then gathered a great crowd of his household servants and searched for the bull everywhere in the wilderness, and at last found it standing on the summit of the lofty mountain, at the entrance of a cave;
and he was then stirred with anger that the bull, going off alone, had forsaken his herd, and he bent his bow and meant to shoot it down with a poisoned arrow;
but the poisoned arrow turned back, as if driven by a blast of wind, and immediately struck down the man who had shot it.
His kinsmen and neighbours were greatly astonished by this event, and none of them dared to go near the bull. So they asked their bishop for advice about what they should do.
The bishop then decided, as counsel for them, that they should pray to God with a fast of three days for a revelation of the miracle.
Then on the third night of the fast the archangel Michael showed himself to the bishop in a spiritual vision, saying,
"You acted wisely in seeking from God what was hidden from men. Know for certain that the man who was shot with his own arrow, it was done by my will.
I am Michael, the archangel of God Almighty, and I always dwell in his sight.
I tell you that I especially love the place that the bull hallowed, and I wished by that sign to make known that I am the guardian of that place;
and of all the signs that happen there I am the overseer and keeper." And with these words the archangel departed to heaven.
The bishop told his vision to the townspeople, and afterwards they habitually went there and earnestly prayed to the living God and to his archangel Michael.
They saw two doors in the church, and the south door was somewhat larger, from which steps lay toward the west side;
but they did not dare to visit the holy house by entering it, but daily prayed earnestly at the door.
Then at that same time the Neapolitans, who were still living in heathenism, declared war against the citizens of the city of Siponto, who honoured the holy place, and against the Beneventans.
They then, taught by their bishop's admonitions, asked for a respite of three days, so that within those three days they might pray with fasting for the help of the archangel Michael.
The heathens likewise, with gifts and offerings, zealously begged protection and defence from their false gods.
Then, on the very night before the battle was to take place in the morning, the archangel Michael showed himself to the bishop,
and said that he had heard their prayers, and promised them his help, and commanded that they should array themselves against their enemies one hour after the third hour of the day.
Then in the morning, glad and free from care because of the angel's promise and trusting in his help, they went out against the heathens.

Then at once, at the beginning of the battle, Mount Garganus was shaking with an immense trembling, and great lightning flew from the mountain like arrows against the heathen people, and the summit of the mountain was entirely overhung with dark mists.

So the heathens took fright and fled. At the same time they were shot with the fiery arrows and pursued from behind by the weapons of the Christians, until they reached their city of Naples half-dead.
Those who escaped these dangers truly recognised that God's angel had come to help the Christians. They immediately bowed their necks to Christ and were armed with his faith.
Six hundred men who had been shot with the fiery arrows were counted among the slain.
Then the victorious Christians returned home with great confidence and joy, and brought the offerings they had vowed to Almighty God and his archangel Michael to the temple.

Then in front of the north door of the church, on the marble stone, they saw what looked like a man's footprints firmly pressed into the stone. They understood that the archangel Michael wished to show this as a sign of his presence.
So they immediately built a church and an altar over it, in praise of the archangel who had stood there helping them in that place.
Then there was great doubt among the citizens about the church: whether they should simply go into it, or whether they ought to consecrate it.
So they built a church in the eastern part of the place and consecrated it in honour of the apostle Peter, and inside it they set up altars to Saint Mary and to John the Baptist.
Then at last the bishop sent to the pope and asked him what he should do about the archangel's building. The pope answered this message thus,
"If men are permitted to consecrate the church which the archangel himself built, then the consecration belongs on the day on which he gave you victory, by the grace of the Almighty.
But if anything else should please the archangel, ask his will on that same day."
When this answer was made known to the bishop, he ordered his citizens to fast for three days, and they prayed to the Holy Trinity that some certain sign might be shown to them about their doubt.
Then on the third night of the fast the archangel Michael said to the bishop in a dream, "You have no need to consecrate the church that I have built.
I myself built it and consecrated it. But go into the church without fear, and, with me standing by, visit the place with prayers according to custom;
and tomorrow you shall sing Mass there, and the people shall go to communion according to divine custom; and then I will show how I consecrated the place myself."
Then early the next morning they came there joyfully with their offerings, and with great steadfastness in their prayers they went in on the south side.
Then they saw a long portico stretching along the north side, nearly up to the marble stone where the angel had stood and shown his footprint.
On the east side a great church was seen, up to which they climbed step by step.
The church with its porch could easily hold five hundred people within its space; and there, set against the middle of the south wall, stood a venerable altar covered with a red cloth.
The building was not built in the way people build, but was angled with various crags, like a cave.
The roof likewise was of varying height: in one place a person could touch it with his head, in another only with difficulty with his hand.
I believe that by this the archangel showed that he sought and loved purity of heart far more than the adornment of stones.
On the outside, the top of the mountain is overgrown with woods in some places and covered with green fields in others.
Truly, after the Mass and the holy communion, everyone returned home with great joy.

Then the bishop settled servants of God there, singers, readers and priests, so that they would carry out God's service there daily in fitting order; and he ordered a monastic dwelling to be built for them there.
Yet no one is bold enough to dare to come into the church at night, only at dawn, when the servants of God sing God's praise inside it.
From the stone of the roof on the north side of the holy altar, very clear and sweet water runs drop by drop, which those who lived in that place called stilla, that is, "drop."
A glass vessel hangs there on a silver chain, and catches the pleasant liquid.
It is the people's custom that after holy communion they climb step by step up to the vessel and taste the heavenly water.
The liquid is very pleasant to the taste and very healing to the touch.
Indeed, very many people, after long fever and various illnesses, quickly regain their health by drinking this liquid.
Likewise, in other ways, countless sick people are often and frequently healed there, and many miracles are performed there through the power of the archangel;
and most of all on this day, when people from every nation visit the place,
and the angel's presence is in some way strongest there, so that the apostle's saying, which he spoke spiritually, may be fulfilled bodily:
he said that "angels are sent hither into the world by God as ministering spirits, to be a help to his chosen, so that they may receive the eternal homeland with them."
The disciples came to Jesus, saying, Who do you think is the greater in the kingdom of heaven: and so on.
Today's gospel says that "the Lord's disciples came to him, saying, Lord, who is the greatest of people in the kingdom of heaven?
Then the Saviour called a little child to him": and so on.
Haymo expounds this gospel, and says how the emperor's tax-collectors, when they were gathering tax for the emperor throughout all the world, asked the apostle Peter; they said,
"Will your teacher Christ pay any tax?" Then Peter said that he would.
Then when Peter wished to ask the Saviour, the Saviour, who knows all things, anticipated him, saying, "What do you think,
Peter: from whom do earthly kings take tribute or tax, from their own kinsmen, or from strangers?" Peter said, "From strangers."
The Saviour said, "Then are their kinsmen free? Lest we offend them, go to the sea and cast out your hook,
and open the mouth of the fish that swallows it first. Then you will find a piece of gold in it. Take that, and give it as toll for me and for you."
Then because he said, "Give it for me and for yourself," the apostles supposed that Peter was the foremost, and they then asked the Saviour,
"Who will be the foremost of men in the kingdom of heaven?" Then the Saviour wished to heal their erroneous thoughts with true humility, and said
that they could not come to the kingdom of heaven unless they were as humble and as innocent as the child whom he had called to him.

An innocent child does not covet other men's possessions, nor a beautiful woman; though it be provoked, it does not hold a long-lasting grudge against the one who harmed it, nor does it dissemble with words, so that it thinks one thing and says another.
So also must God's followers, that is, Christians, have in their minds the innocence that a child has in its age.
The Saviour said, "Truly I say to you, you will not come to the kingdom of heaven unless you are turned and become like little children."
He did not command his disciples to be children in body, but to keep the innocence of guileless children in their conduct.
In another place, when a child was brought to him to be blessed and his disciples complained about it, he said, "Allow these children to come to me; truly, of such is the kingdom of heaven."
Concerning this the apostle Paul admonished those under his charge, and said, "Do not be children in understanding, but in wickedness; be perfect in understanding."
The Saviour said, "Whoever humbles himself like this child will be foremost in the kingdom of heaven."
Let us have true humility in our life, if we wish to have high honour in God's kingdom; as the Saviour said,
"Everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and he who humbles himself shall be exalted."
He has the innocence of a guileless child who is displeasing to himself so that he may be pleasing to God;
and he is so much the more beautiful in God's sight as he is the more humble in his own sight.
"He who receives one such little one in my name receives me myself."
Good deeds should be done for all God's poor, but most of all for the humble and gentle, who agree with Christ's commandments in the conduct of their lives;
for he is served when his poor are served, and he himself is received when they are received.
He also said in another place, "He who receives a prophet will have a prophet's reward; he who receives a righteous man will have a righteous man's reward."
That is, whoever receives a prophet or some righteous servant of God, and provides him with food for the love of God,
will have as great a reward from God for his generosity as if he himself were a prophet or a righteous servant of God.
"Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him that a huge millstone were tied to his neck, and that he were thus sunk in the deep sea."
He offends another who deceives him in the things of God, so that his soul is lost.
The millstone, which turns continually and completes no journey, signifies love of the world, which circles about in errors and sets no firm step on God's way.
Of such men the prophet said, "The wicked go round in a circle."
He who comes into holy orders in God's church, and afterwards sets others an evil example through wicked enticement or a sinful way of life,
and overturns their understanding, then it would be better for him to perish alone in a worldly way of life than, in a holy habit, to draw others with him to perdition through his perverse conduct.
"Woe to the world because of offences." Here "the world" means those who love this perishing world more than eternal life, and who ruin themselves and others with various deceits.
"It must needs be that offences come; nevertheless, woe to the man by whom they come."
This world is so filled with errors that it cannot be without offences; and yet woe to the man who cheats another of his possessions
or of his life; and it is worse for the one who, with evil incitements, deceives another man's soul into eternal perdition.
"If your hand or your foot offends you, cut off that limb and cast it from you." This is said according to a spiritual meaning, not according to a bodily rule.
God did not command any man to mutilate his limbs. The hand signifies our needful friend, who daily meets our needs with work and help;

but even so, if such a friend turns us aside from God's way, then it is better for us to cut his fleshly love away from us and cast it off by separation, than that we, through his evil incitement, should fall together with him into eternal perdition.
So it is also with the foot and with the eye. If some kinsman is as dear to you as your eye, and another as useful as your hand, and one as serviceable as your own foot,
if they then perversely incite you to the ruin of your soul, then it is better for you to shun their fellowship than that they should lead you onward with them to eternal perdition.
"Take heed that you do not despise one of these little ones." He who deceives one of God's servants angers the Lord, as he himself said through his prophet,
"He who touches you, it is as grievous to me as if he touched the pupil of my eye."
"I say to you that their angels always see the face of my Father, who is in heaven." By these words it is made clear that an angel is appointed as guardian to every faithful person,
who shields him against the devil's snares and helps him in holy virtues, just as the psalmist said concerning every righteous man,
"God has commanded his angels concerning you, that they keep you and bear you up in their hands, lest you strike your foot against a stone."
Great is the honour of Christian people, that each one has, from his birth, an angel entrusted to him for guardianship, as is written concerning the apostle Peter,
when the angel led him out of the prison, and he came to his companions and, knocking, asked to be let in. Then the faithful said,
"It is not Peter who is knocking there, but it is his angel." Truly the angels whom God has appointed as guardians to his chosen ones never depart from his presence;
for God is everywhere, and wherever the angels fly, they are always within his presence and enjoy his glory.
They make known our works and prayers to the Almighty, though nothing is hidden from him, just as the archangel Raphael said to the man of God, Tobias,
"When you prayed, I offered your prayers before God."
The Old Law tells us that archangels are set over every nation, above the other angels, to watch over that people, as Moses showed in these words in the fifth book of the Old Law:
"When the most high God divided and scattered the offspring of Adam, he set the boundaries of the nations according to the number of his angels."
The prophet Daniel agrees with this meaning in his prophecy. An angel of God spoke to Daniel about the archangel who governed the Persian nation, and said,
"The archangel, the prince of the Greek nation, came to me, and none of them is my helper except Michael, the prince of the Hebrew people.
Behold, now Michael, one of the foremost princes, came to help me, and I remained there against the king of the Persian nation."
These words show how much care the archangels take over their authority over mankind, when he said that Michael came to help him.
It is now credible that the archangel Michael, who was the prince of the Hebrew people while they believed in God, has the care of Christian people;
and he made that clear when he built a church for himself among a faithful nation, on Mount Gargano, as we read a little earlier.

It is arranged by God's ordinance that the glorious heavenly angel is always the helper of Christian people on earth, and their intercessor in heaven with Almighty God, who lives and reigns forever in eternity. Amen.
